function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse, the sample matrix, the required sensitivity, and the downstream instrumentation. Below is a quick guide to help you decide which technique might suit your needs best.** | Ionisation Technique | Typical Use‑Cases | Strengths | Weaknesses | When to Choose It | |----------------------|-------------------|-----------|------------|-------------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Small, volatile, thermally stable molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, pesticides). | • Robust, reproducible fragmentation patterns.
• Good for library matching.
• No matrix effects. | • Requires high vacuum.
• Not suitable for large biomolecules.
• Limited to volatile compounds. | When you need a *standardised* fragmentation pattern for library identification (e.g., GC‑MS). | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Semi‑volatile organics, polar compounds. | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation.
• Can produce protonated or deprotonated ions.
• Useful for quantitation. | • Requires a reagent gas (CH₄, NH₃, etc.).
• Still needs GC‑MS. | When you need *intact* molecular ions for accurate mass determination or when EI fragments too much. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Small to medium‑size polar/non‑polar molecules, pharmaceuticals, metabolites. | • Works with LC‑MS.
• Handles moderately polar compounds.
• Good for quantitative work. | • Less effective for very polar or large biomolecules.
• Requires a nebuliser. | When you need a *robust* ionisation for routine LC‑MS analysis of drugs, metabolites, or environmental contaminants. | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides, nucleic acids), polar metabolites, complex mixtures. | • Very soft → preserves non‑covalent complexes.
• Produces multiply charged ions → extends mass range.
• Compatible with LC‑MS. | • Susceptible to ion suppression from salts or detergents.
• Requires careful optimisation of solvent composition. | When analysing *large, polar, or highly charged* molecules, especially in proteomics, metabolomics, or complex biological samples. | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteins, peptides, polymers, large biomolecules, imaging mass spectrometry. | • Minimal sample prep.
• High throughput.
• Good for imaging (MALDI‑IMS). | • Requires a suitable matrix.
• Lower mass resolution compared to FT‑ICR or Orbitrap. | When you need *rapid screening* of large biomolecules or spatial localisation (imaging). | | **Laser Desorption/Ionisation (LDI) / LDI‑TOF** | Polymers, inorganic materials, nanoparticles. | • No matrix needed.
• Simple setup. | • Limited to non‑polar, high‑mass species. | When you want to analyse *non‑polar* high‑mass materials without matrix interference. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | Non‑polar, aromatic compounds, PAHs, pharmaceuticals. | • Works well with non‑polar analytes.
• Less ion suppression than APCI. | • Requires a UV lamp.
• Not ideal for very polar compounds. | When you need to ionise *non‑polar* or *aromatic* molecules that are poorly ionised by APCI/ESI. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoelectron Spectroscopy (APPS)** | Surface‑analysis, thin films, polymers. | • Provides surface‑sensitive ionisation.
• Useful for studying polymer degradation. | • Requires specialised equipment. | When you need *surface‑specific* ionisation for polymer or thin‑film studies. | --- ### Quick Decision Flow 1. **What’s the sample?** - *Small, volatile*: EI or CI (GC‑MS). - *Large, polar, biomolecule*: ESI (LC‑MS). - *Large, non‑polar, polymer*: MALDI or LDI. 2. **What’s the goal?** - *Library identification*: EI (GC‑MS). - *Quantitation*: CI, APCI, or ESI (depending on polarity). - *Imaging*: MALDI‑IMS. - *Surface analysis*: APPS. 3. **Instrument availability** - If you have a GC‑MS → EI/CI. - If you have an LC‑MS → ESI/APCI/APPI. - If you have a MALDI‑TOF → MALDI. 4. **Matrix effects** - ESI is most susceptible; use APCI/APPI for less polar matrices. 5. **Mass range** - ESI can handle very high masses (up to 200 kDa) due to multiple charging. - MALDI also handles high masses but typically produces singly charged ions. --- ### Bottom Line - **For routine small‑molecule analysis**: **EI** (GC‑MS) or **APCI** (LC‑MS). - **For large biomolecules**: **ESI** (LC‑MS) or **MALDI** (TOF‑MS). - **For non‑polar, aromatic compounds**: **APPI** (LC‑MS). - **For imaging or spatial localisation**: **MALDI‑IMS**. If you give me more details about your sample type, analytical goals, and available instrumentation, I can narrow down the recommendation even further!
